vopros: What do foreign nationals need to buy a home in Los Angeles?

vyzhimka.tekst:
Yes. Foreign nationals can generally buy residential real estate in Los Angeles; U.S. citizenship, a green card, or California residency is not generally a prerequisite to owning a home. The bigger differences are financing, documentation, taxes, and how you structure ownership.

For a typical purchase, you should expect to need:

- Identification: Usually a valid foreign passport and proof of your overseas address. Escrow/title and banks may request additional identity documents for compliance purposes.
- Funds: If paying cash, you'll need to demonstrate and transfer the purchase funds through channels acceptable to escrow/title. Be prepared to document the source of substantial international transfers.
- Financing, if applicable: This is usually the biggest hurdle. Foreign-national mortgage programs exist, but their requirements differ from ordinary U.S. mortgages. A lender may require a larger down payment, proof of foreign income/assets, bank statements, credit references, and reserves. California's DRE notes that financing generally depends on factors such as credit history, employment stability and down payment. ([dre.ca.gov](https://www.dre.ca.gov/Consumers/FirstHomeCalifornia.html?utm_source=openai))
- An ITIN/SSN when required for tax purposes: You don't automatically need an SSN just because you're purchasing property. A foreign person who isn't eligible for an SSN may use an IRS Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (ITIN) when U.S. tax rules require one. An ITIN does not confer immigration status or work authorization. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/tin/itin/itin-supporting-documents?utm_source=openai))
- Escrow and title: California transactions normally use an escrow company and title company to handle funds, documents, title transfer and title insurance. ([dre.ca.gov](https://www.dre.ca.gov/consumers/informationforhomebuyers.html?utm_source=openai))
- Buyer representation agreement: If you hire a buyer's agent, California law now requires a written buyer-broker representation agreement no later than when your offer is executed. ([dre.ca.gov](https://dre.ca.gov/Consumers/ConsumerAlert_20241114_Changes_to_Real_Estate_Representation.html?utm_source=openai))

There are also important tax considerations. Owning U.S. real estate can create U.S. federal and California tax obligations, particularly if you rent the property. Rental income earned by a nonresident alien is subject to specific U.S. tax rules. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/nonresident-aliens-real-property-located-in-the-us?utm_source=openai)) When a foreign owner eventually sells U.S. real estate, FIRPTA can require the buyer/closing party to withhold generally 15% of the amount realized, subject to exceptions and reduced-withholding procedures. California has separate real-estate withholding rules as well. ([irs.gov](https://www.irs.gov/individuals/international-taxpayers/firpta-withholding?utm_source=openai))

One thing worth deciding before making the purchase is who will legally own the property: you personally, an LLC, a trust, a foreign corporation, etc. For a foreign national, that decision can have significant U.S. income-tax and estate-tax consequences, so it shouldn't be made solely for convenience.

If you tell me your nationality/residence, whether you're buying with cash or a mortgage, approximate LA purchase price, and whether this will be your home, vacation property, or rental investment, I can lay out the specific documents, down payment, taxes, and expected closing costs for your situation.
